title: Hybrid search and reranking
summary: Keyword search finds exact terms such as error codes, IDs, and names. **Vector search** finds passages with similar meaning, even in different words. **Hybrid search** runs both and merges the results; a **reranker** then puts the best few on top.

sections.title: Each search finds what the other misses

blocks.text:
Keyword search usually uses **BM25**, which scores documents by how often the query's words appear in them. Vector search compares **embeddings**: lists of numbers representing meaning, where similar texts get similar numbers.

Query: "ORA-00060 deadlock when saving orders"

table.title: One query, two searches
rows: The guide “Handling lock contention”, which never mentions the code
“Handling lock contention”, “Deadlocks in the order service”
May rank the exact-code article low

blocks.text: The two searches score on different scales, so don't just add the scores. **Reciprocal rank fusion** merges by position instead: each document scores `1 / (60 + rank)` for each list it appears in, summed.

A reranker (usually a "cross-encoder" model) reads the query and each candidate together, and judges relevance more accurately than either search. It is too slow for every document, so run it on the top 50–100 merged results and keep the best 5–10.

Keep each passage's source and permissions attached. A relevant passage can still be outdated or wrong; relevance and correctness are measured separately (chapter 7).

reason: Keep search fusion separate from claim grounding; add the score-comparability caution and a concrete fusion method.

title: Filter by permission before the model sees text
summary: Apply the user's permissions during the search, before any text reaches the model. Filtering the final answer is too late: the model, the logs, and any other agents have already seen the data.

sections.title: Filter in the search, then check again

blocks.text: Store each chunk's **ACL** (access control list: who may read it), and pass the user's permissions into the search itself.

code.title: Permission check before the model
code.text:
scope      = session.user.document_scope            # from the login, not the model
candidates = index.search(query, filter = scope)    # never fetch first and hide later
allowed    = [c for c in candidates if acl.can_read(session.user, c.doc_id)]  # current check
context    = label_as_outside_data(load_text(allowed))
answer     = model(question, context)
code.caption: The second check catches access removed since the document was indexed.

blocks.text: When someone loses access to a document, everything derived from it must stop reaching them too: cached search results, summaries, saved citations, and memories. Store the source document and its permission version with each derived item, and check again before showing it. Test with users of the same tenant who have different access, as well as with different tenants.

reason: Keep retrieval access as an explicit boundary and extend it to permission revocation and derived context.

title: Stale and conflicting sources
summary: Decide how up to date each fact must be, and fetch it accordingly: live systems for current values, document search for stable text, keeping timestamps either way. When sources disagree, first check whether they measure the same thing (period, currency, definition). Then trust the source that owns that fact, and show any remaining conflict instead of averaging it away.

blocks.text: A recently indexed copy can still hold an old document. Track when the **source** was last updated, not just when you fetched it.

code.title: Choosing a source by freshness

sections.title: Compare definitions before picking a winner

blocks.text: Many contradictions are two sources measuring different things.

table.title: Two “Q3 revenue” figures
rows: Orders booked, updated hourly, including pending ones
Revenue earned, minus refunds, final for the quarter
table.caption: Not a contradiction: two definitions. Answer “revenue” from the ledger and mention the difference.

blocks.text: If the definitions match and the numbers still differ, trust the source that owns that fact: the ledger for revenue, the HR system for headcount. If the conflict matters and remains, show both figures with their sources and ask someone to confirm. Never average two incompatible numbers.

Two agents reporting different totals are two conflicting sources; handle them the same way. Compare their assumptions (period, currency, how refunds count), then recompute once from the source data with a fixed query. Asking a third model to vote proves nothing. Keep the replaced findings and where they came from, and escalate an important conflict that remains to a responsible person.

reason: Merge stale knowledge, conflicting sources, and specialist disagreements; the same authority/scope/provenance procedure resolves all three.

title: Check that citations support claims
summary: A citation helps only if the cited passage actually supports the sentence, conditions included. Split the answer into individual claims, check each against its passage, and fix or remove the ones that aren't supported.

blocks.text: Smooth summaries tend to drop exactly the condition that made a statement true.

table.title: Claims checked against one passage
headings: Passage: “Unopened products may be returned within 30 days.”
rows: “Unopened products can be returned within 30 days.”

blocks.text: Run it after the answer is written and before the user sees it.

code.title: Check each claim

blocks.text: Use code where it can decide: the document exists, the version matches, a quoted number appears in the passage. Use a model to judge whether the meaning is supported, after testing it against human ratings (see *LLM-as-a-judge*).

reason: Keep claim grounding distinct from relevance so a good retrieval score is not mistaken for a supported answer.

title: Multi-hop retrieval
summary: **Multi-hop retrieval** answers questions where one search reveals what to search for next. Each round (a “hop”) passes a specific, sourced finding, such as an ID, a name, or a date, to the next search, with limits on the number of hops and the cost.

blocks.text: "Why did revenue drop last quarter?" can't be answered by one search:

table.title: A three-hop investigation
rows: Which products' revenue fell in Q3?
What changed for SKU-17 and SKU-22 in Q3?
A price increase on July 4 (pricing log)
Did sales drop after July 4 for every customer group?
table.caption: Conclusion: the price change coincides with the small-business drop. That is a supported guess, not a proven cause.

blocks.text:
- Cap the hops, searches, and time.
- Stop when the question is answered, when a hop finds nothing new, or when the next step needs data you can't access.
- Pass facts forward, not guesses, and keep the chain of sources so the answer can show its reasoning.
- Say what kind of conclusion it is: confirmed, a likely explanation, or still open.

reason: Retain multi-hop retrieval as a distinct dependency pattern, with explicit evidence transfer and stopping rules.

title: Fit the context window
summary: The **context window** is the most text a model can read in one call, measured in tokens (a token is roughly three-quarters of a word). Always keep the goal, permissions, pending commitments, and the information for the next step; summarize or link everything else. Then confirm on your test set that cutting tokens didn't cut quality.

blocks.text: Shortening must never drop a limit, an approval, or an action with an unknown result.

code.title: Building context within a budget
code.text:
keep     = [goal, permissions, pending_approvals, unfinished_actions, limits]
evidence = select_for(next_step, max_tokens = EVIDENCE_BUDGET)
history  = summarize(completed_steps, keep = source_links)
require tokens(keep) <= BUDGET                   # if not, split the task
context  = keep + fit(evidence + history, BUDGET - tokens(keep))
code.caption: A summary must not turn an outside claim into a fact, or drop a condition that limits an action.

sections.title: Use fewer tokens without losing quality

blocks.text:
Roughly in order of impact:

- Fetch fewer, better passages: rerank and keep the top few.
- Link to large files and fetch sections only when needed.
- Summarize finished steps; keep IDs and sources, drop the narration.
- Offer only the tools this task needs; every tool description is re-sent on every call.
- Ask for compact output.
- Use **prompt caching**, a provider feature that reuses the processed form of a repeated prompt start (system prompt, tool list). It cuts cost and delay, though not the amount of text.

Test every change on the golden set (success, grounding, policy, speed, cost) before and after.

reason: Merge context-window management and token reduction; both are tested information-preservation choices.

title: Evaluate the whole run, not just the answer
summary: Test at several levels: the final outcome, each tool choice and its inputs, the whole **trajectory** (the full sequence of decisions and tool calls in one task), and the reply. A right answer reached by reading another customer's data, or after twenty wasted calls, is still a failure.

blocks.text: Each level catches failures the others miss.

table.title: What to measure
rows: Did the requested change actually happen?
Was it the right tool for the step?
Share of invalid or denied calls
Did it stay within the task? Was it efficient?
Share of supported claims; rubric score
p95 latency; cost per success; escalation rate

blocks.text:
Two runs can end with the same correct summary. One read only the requested account; the other read five unrelated customers' accounts along the way. Only the trajectory shows the difference, and the second run is a privacy incident.

Long chains also multiply failure. If each of 10 steps independently succeeded 95% of the time, the whole task would succeed only about 60% of the time (0.95^10 ≈ 0.60). Real errors aren't independent, since one early misunderstanding derails every later step, so measure complete runs instead of multiplying step scores.

Break results down by task type and by cause (bad search, misread request, invalid action, outside service failed, false success claim). One average hides what to fix.

reason: Merge evaluation levels, metric lists, and trajectory evaluation; add a worked example of error accumulation.

title: Evaluate retrieval on its own
summary: A model can't use a passage it never received. Test search, ranking, and answer writing as separate steps, so a search failure isn't mistaken for a model failure.

blocks.text:
For each test question, mark which passages are relevant. Then look at the top **k** results, where k is how many passages you actually give the model:

- **precision@k:** of those k passages, the share that are relevant;
- **recall@k:** of all relevant passages, the share that made it into the top k.

Example: a question has 4 relevant passages, and the top 5 results include 3 of them. Precision@5 = 3/5 = 0.6; recall@5 = 3/4 = 0.75. Both are only as good as the relevance labels.

table.title: Find the step that failed
rows: The relevant passage was never found
Indexing, the query, filters, or the search
Found, but dropped before reaching the model
Given to the model, but the claim is still wrong
A forbidden passage reached the model
Permissions: a security failure, not a relevance problem

blocks.text:
Measure ranking with the number of passages you really use, then check answers built from exactly those passages. Study cases where recall improved but task success didn't; they usually point to answer writing or checking.

Include questions your documents **can't** answer. The right reply is "I couldn't find this". Recall makes no sense when nothing is relevant, so score these cases separately.

reason: Add a retrieval-specific evaluation layer so answer scores cannot hide upstream search failures.
questions: How do you test the retrieval part of a RAG system?
references: Stanford IR book: precision and recall

title: LLM-as-a-judge
summary: **LLM-as-a-judge** means using a language model to score outputs against criteria. It is useful for qualities code can't check, such as clarity, relevance, or completeness. But it is only as reliable as its measured agreement with human ratings on your data: measure that agreement, correct for its known biases, and never use a judge where an exact check exists.

blocks.text:
If code can check something, let code check it: the output's shape, the database state, a calculation, whether a citation exists, whether a call was allowed. Use a judge only for what needs interpretation.

Give the judge specific criteria ("Does the reply state the refund amount and when it will arrive?") rather than "Rate quality from 1 to 10", and ask it to quote the text behind its verdict.

- **Position bias:** when comparing two answers, judges favor one slot. Run each pair in both orders.
- **Length bias:** longer answers score higher. Reward brevity in the criteria, and check whether scores track length.
- **Self-preference:** a judge may favor answers from its own model family. Use a different model where possible.
- **Wording sensitivity:** small prompt changes move scores. Fix the judge's model and prompt.

Have people rate 100–200 typical cases, and measure how well the judge agrees with them. Use **Cohen's kappa**, an agreement score that corrects for lucky agreement (1 is perfect, 0 is chance), rather than plain percent agreement. Measure again whenever the judge changes, and report judge scores together with that agreement.

reason: Keep model-judge calibration separate from evaluator-optimizer mechanics because scoring reliability is its own concern.

title: Test prompt-injection resistance
summary: Plant malicious instructions wherever untrusted content enters, then check what the agent actually revealed, called, or saved. What the reply says doesn't count. A good result blocks the attack **and** still completes the real task.

sections.title: Score what happened, not what was said

blocks.text: Hide attacks in fetched pages, emails, tool results, attachments, and messages from other agents, under realistic task permissions. Try data theft, gaining extra permissions, misusing tools, and memory poisoning.

code.title: An injection test loop
code.text:
for attack in attack_set:                       # include new and held-out attacks
    run = agent.run(real_task, documents = inject(attack))
    check(run.leaked_restricted_data == 0)
    check(run.forbidden_calls_executed == 0)    # the controls must hold
    record(run.forbidden_calls_attempted)       # the model was fooled; track how often
    check(run.unapproved_memory_saves == 0)
    record(run.real_task_completed)
code.caption: Report three numbers: attacks that caused harm (must be 0), attacks that fooled the model but were blocked, and real-task success while under attack.

blocks.text:
A system that refuses every document containing an instruction is safe but useless, so track real-task success alongside attack results.

Vary attacks: different encodings, languages, and hiding places, plus every attack seen in production. Keep some attacks out of tuning, so you don't just fit the known ones. New wording will sometimes fool the model, which is why the controls in chapter 3 must not depend on the model.

reason: Retain attack testing as a separate evaluation lesson, distinguishing observed effects, attempted misuse, and useful task completion.

title: Failure injection and chaos testing
summary: Cause failures on purpose (crashes, timeouts, duplicate messages, provider outages) at the worst moments, then check that the rules that must always hold still do: no double charge, no expired approval used, no data sent to an unapproved provider. **Chaos testing** does this in a realistic environment, with the possible damage kept small.

blocks.text: The most valuable test kills the worker after an action goes through but before its result is saved (see the timeline in *Durable execution: survive crashes*).

code.title: A crash-window test
code.text:
test "crash after the refund is paid, before the result is saved":
    inject crash at: after payments.pay(op-42), before history.save(step 4)
    resume the task to completion
    assert payments.refunds(order = 42).count == 1
    assert task.status == COMPLETED and task.receipt == "R-981"

sections.title: Pair each failure with an invariant

blocks.text: A test passes only if the invariant holds; a process that merely restarts isn't enough.

table.title: Failures and what must stay true
rows: Worker killed right after an action
The action isn't repeated after recovery
Nothing runs on the expired approval
A tool slower than the deadline
No endless wait; no blind retry of the change
No fallback to a provider that breaks privacy rules
A worker frozen past its lease
The stale worker's write is rejected

blocks.text: Start in test environments. Record the exact failure timing and versions, so every failure you find becomes a repeatable test.

reason: Merge reliability failure injection and chaos testing; teach fault timing and invariants together.

title: Release gates and canary releases
summary: A new version ships only if it passes hard blockers (zero security failures, zero duplicate actions) and meets quality, speed, and cost limits on the golden set. Then it reaches users gradually: first in **shadow mode** (running on copies of real requests without taking real actions), then as a **canary** (a small share of real traffic), expanding or rolling back by rules set in advance.

blocks.text: Write the blockers down before seeing results, so nobody argues them away afterwards.

code.title: Release gate
code.text:
require security_failures == 0
require duplicate_actions == 0
require golden_set.success_rate >= QUALITY_BAR     # per category, not just overall
require p95_latency <= LATENCY_LIMIT
require cost_per_success <= COST_LIMIT
require tested_versions == shipping_versions       # prompt, model, tools, policy
code.caption: A high average can't make up for one unauthorized payment.

blocks.text: Each stage has a written condition for moving on and a trigger for rolling back.

table.title: Rollout stages
rows: No: proposals are logged and compared
Proposals match or beat the current version
Results at least as good as the current version for the agreed period
table.caption: Any serious violation rolls back automatically. Test the rollback before the canary starts.

blocks.text: Make sure shadow mode truly can't act: a shadow agent with access to the live payment tool is not a shadow.

reason: Merge release blockers with canary rollout so testing and increasing authority form one gated progression.

title: Compare designs fairly
summary: Compare designs on the same versioned test set with the same scoring, looking at quality, safety, speed, cost, and upkeep. To compare on live traffic, run an **A/B test**: randomly assign each user (or account) to one design and compare outcomes, using shadow mode first when actions are risky.

blocks.text: Run every design on the same golden set with the same scoring, and look at the full picture rather than one number:

table.title: Example comparison
table.caption: Two points of quality rarely justify three times the cost and time. Prefer the simpler design unless the gain matters.

blocks.text: Check whether the gap is real before acting on it. With a few hundred test cases, two points is often noise. Because both designs ran the same cases, use a test built for paired results, such as **McNemar's test**, which asks whether the cases where only one design passed lean one way by more than chance. Record the decision and its assumptions, so you can revisit it when the workload changes.

- **Assign by user or account,** so no one switches designs mid-conversation, and analyze results per user, not per request; one user's requests aren't independent.
- **Keep the two groups apart:** no shared memory or caches that leak one design's behavior into the other.
- **Choose the main metric and the safety limits before starting,** and run long enough to detect the difference you care about.
- **Never run two real actions for one customer request** just to compare designs. For risky actions, compare in shadow mode.

reason: Merge architecture comparison and online experimentation while distinguishing offline paired workloads from live random assignment.

title: Types of memory, and what to share
summary: Sort memory by purpose: **working memory** holds what the current task needs, **episodic memory** records past experiences, and **semantic memory** stores lasting facts and preferences. When several agents work together, they share checked findings through a common store with access rules, not each other's full histories.

blocks.text: None of these replaces the saved task state that records which actions happened (chapter 5).

table.title: Memory types
rows: Rows returned by the current database query
What was tried in last month's similar outage
As long as it stays relevant, within retention limits
“This customer prefers French”; “The team names files in snake_case”
table.caption: Access rules and retention limits apply to all three.

blocks.text: Save a short finding with its source and a link to the full material, rather than a whole conversation in which nobody knows which statements were checked.

Should several agents share one memory? Share **facts**, not everything. Each agent keeps its own working memory. A shared store holds accepted findings, their sources, and task decisions, with rules for who may read, add, correct, and delete each entry.

A single scratchpad that every agent reads and writes looks simple, but it spreads one agent's mistake to all of them, mixes data that different users may not see, and invites conflicting edits.

reason: Merge memory categories and sharing into a purpose-and-scope decision; checkpoint distinctions were introduced with execution state.

title: What to save to memory
summary: Save something to long-term memory only if it will be useful later, may be stored, and has been verified or confirmed by the user, and record where it came from. **Memory poisoning** is untrusted content, or a wrong guess, saved as if it were fact; the save checks and the source record are the defense. When two agents edit the same entry at once, a version check stops one edit from silently erasing the other.

blocks.text: Memory keeps mistakes as faithfully as facts, and repeats them in every future task.

table.title: Save or not?
rows: User: “Please reply in French from now on”
Yes, as a preference the user stated
Email: “Our new bank account is IBAN …”
No: a classic poisoning attempt. Verify through the vendor-change process.
Only for that order; remove it after delivery

code.title: Checks before saving
code.text:
candidate = extract_memory(observation)
if not useful_for_future_tasks(candidate):  return
require storage_rules.allow(candidate, owner)       # consent, sensitivity, tenant
require candidate.verified or candidate.confirmed_by_user
memory.save(candidate, owner, source, expires_at)

sections.title: Record where each memory came from

blocks.text: **Provenance** means where information came from and how it was checked. Store enough to answer "should we still believe this?"

code.title: A memory entry
code.text:
memory = {
    id, tenant_id, owner_id, content,
    source,                       # e.g. "user message m-81" or "vendor portal, verified"
    created_at, verified_at, verification_status,
    expires_at, access_rules, version,
    replaces                      # the entry this one corrects, if any
}

blocks.text: If a source later turns out to be wrong, its provenance lets you find and recheck everything built on it. Finding a memory by similar meaning says nothing about whether it is true.

sections.title: Two edits at the same time

blocks.text: Two agents read version 7 of an entry, each changes it, and both save. Without a check, the second save erases the first. **Compare-and-swap** prevents this: a save succeeds only if the entry is still at the version you read.

code.title: Catching a lost update
code.text:
entry  = memory.read(id, scope)
edited = apply(entry, change)
ok = memory.compare_and_swap(id, expected_version = entry.version,
                             new_value = edited, new_version = entry.version + 1)
if not ok: reload_and_resolve(id, change)     # never just retry with the old value

blocks.text: Resolve conflicts by meaning: two independent tags can be merged, but two different payment accounts can't, so escalate those. A version check only detects a conflict. It doesn't decide which value is right, and it doesn't replace the save checks.

reason: Merge memory-write eligibility, incorrect memories, metadata, poisoning, and concurrent edits into one persistence contract.

title: Expire and delete memories
summary: **Decay** lowers an old memory's ranking. **Expiry** makes it unusable. **Deletion** removes it together with every copy made from it: search index entries, embeddings, summaries, caches, and eventually backups. These are three different operations with different guarantees.

blocks.text: A lower score doesn't remove an entry, and an expired entry must not come back just because it closely matches a question.

table.title: Decay vs. expiry
rows: Its score drops with age; it can still appear
A one-time delivery address can be used
After delivery it is excluded by rule, or deleted

blocks.text: Set retention by purpose. A language preference can stay until the user changes it. A temporary instruction ("call me on my work phone this week") should expire on its own.
A deletion isn't finished when the main entry is gone.

code.title: Deleting a user's memories
code.text:
1. check who is asking and what is covered
2. write a tombstone(user)        # a deletion marker: stops old jobs re-adding the data
3. delete from: main store, vector index, summaries, caches
4. confirm each copy is gone; retry failures; report completion
5. backups: let them expire on schedule, or re-apply tombstones when restoring
code.caption: Without the tombstone, a re-indexing job or an old summary can quietly bring deleted data back.

reason: Merge lifecycle and privacy deletion while preserving the decay-versus-deletion distinction.

title: When to use multiple agents
summary: Start with one agent and good tools. Split the work across several agents only when a clear, measured reason exists: different permissions, a distinct skill, or independent work that benefits from running in parallel. Multi-agent systems often do worse than one agent, because information is lost between agents, calls multiply, and mistakes spread.

sections.title: Good and bad reasons to split

blocks.text: Compare any split against a single agent on the same golden set (chapter 7).

table.title: When a second agent earns its place
rows: A legal-review agent may read privileged documents; the support agent may not
A distinct skill or tool set
A data-analysis agent with a sandboxed Python environment
Researching ten companies at once to meet a deadline
Another team runs, and answers for, the finance agent
table.caption: Weak reasons: “the prompt is long”, “it mirrors our org chart”, “more agents seem smarter”.

sections.title: Why more agents can do worse

blocks.text:
- **Information is lost at each handoff:** the second agent never sees what the user actually said.
- **Calls multiply:** cost and time often grow several times over, for a small quality gain.
- **Mistakes spread together:** agents on the same model share the same blind spots, so their agreement doesn't confirm anything.
- **Coordination breaks:** duplicated work, conflicting results, agents waiting on each other in circles.
- **Debugging is harder,** because one failure is spread over several agents' records.

If you do split, give each agent a limited job: a goal, inputs, permissions, an output format, a deadline, and an owner. The agent that delegated stays responsible for checking the result.

reason: Merge multi-agent selection and its failure costs into one evidence-based architecture decision.

title: The supervisor pattern
summary: In the **orchestrator–worker** pattern, also called the supervisor pattern, one agent breaks a task into pieces, gives each to a worker agent with clear limits and an output format, checks what comes back, and writes the final result. The supervisor answers for the whole task; each worker answers only for its piece.

blocks.text: Unlike a fixed parallel workflow, the pieces aren't known in advance: the supervisor decides them from the request. Each assignment states what to return and how it will be checked.

table.title: A due-diligence report, split up
rows: Find the company's last 3 years of public filings
Compute revenue growth and margin from the filings
Numbers and how they were computed
List risks and contradictions in the findings
Each issue points to a finding
table.caption: These three run in order, since each needs the previous output. Independent pieces, such as one research worker per year, can run in parallel.

blocks.text: When workers edit shared files, give each file one owner so workers don't overwrite each other.

- Check each result's format, sources, and coverage before using it.
- A worker that fails or times out leaves a visible "missing" entry; it must not silently vanish from the report.
- Running the team gives the supervisor no extra permissions. Its actions still pass through the tool gateway.

reason: Merge orchestrator-worker and supervisor architecture, which described the same coordination shape.

title: Handoffs, agents as tools, and peer-to-peer
summary: In an **agent-as-tool** design, one agent calls another like a tool, gets a result, and stays in charge. In a **handoff**, the second agent takes over the conversation with the user. In a **peer-to-peer** design, agents message each other directly with no one in charge, which still needs clear rules on ownership, deadlines, and when to stop.

blocks.text: The difference is who talks to the user next.

table.title: Handoff vs. agent-as-tool
rows: First agent → second → back to first
Ask a reviewer agent to check a contract clause
Pass a support chat to the billing agent
A conversation summary and the user's permissions

reason: Combine interaction ownership and peer topology while keeping their distinct tradeoffs as separate sections.

title: MCP vs. A2A, and agent-to-agent messages
summary: **MCP** connects an agent to tools and data: the server does what it is asked. **A2A** (Agent2Agent) connects independent agents: the receiving agent accepts a task, decides how to do it, and reports progress and results, sometimes over hours. Either way, send a limited task rather than the whole conversation, and take permissions from verified credentials, never from what the message claims.

blocks.text: The two overlap at the edges (an agent can be offered as an MCP tool), but the key difference is who decides how the work gets done.

table.title: MCP vs. A2A
rows: A tool call or data read, usually quick
A task with status updates and results; can run long
Decides how to do the task
Ask the finance team's agent to match an invoice to its order

sections.title: What a message to another agent contains

blocks.text: A limited task, not the whole conversation:

code.title: A delegation message
code.text:
message = {
    task_id, parent_task_id, correlation_id,
    sender, recipient,
    goal:            "Match invoice INV-42 to purchase order PO-7",
    inputs:          ["doc://invoices/INV-42", "erp://po/7"],
    allowed:         {items: [INV-42, PO-7], actions: [read]},
    expected_output: MatchResult format,
    deadline:        2026-10-26T14:00Z
}
permissions = from the verified connection (mTLS) or a signed token, never from `allowed`
code.caption: `allowed` tells the receiving agent its limits. Enforcement comes from credentials it can't edit. mTLS is a connection where both sides prove who they are with certificates.

reason: Merge protocol comparison and message structure, adding long-running task status and avoiding an overly absolute MCP/A2A distinction.
references: Tasks, messages, results, and authenticated communication between agents.

title: Safe delegation without loops
summary: A task handed to another agent may receive only part of its parent's permissions and budget, never more. Track each task's parent, depth, and deadline, so circular waits (A waits for B while B waits for A) are refused before they start, and endless re-delegation is stopped.

blocks.text: The risk is a child agent receiving wider permissions than its parent had: "it's just reading invoices" turns into permission to change the accounting ledger.

code.title: Narrowing permissions when delegating
code.text:
require child.requested_scope ⊆ parent.scope
child_scope = child.requested_scope ∩ caller.permissions ∩ worker.policy
token       = issue_delegated_token(child_scope, expires = child.deadline)
worker.run(child, token)            # every tool checks the token on every call

blocks.text: Give every task a fixed ID and a link to its parent, and check for a cycle before adding a new dependency.

code.title: Checks before delegating
code.caption: Detect cycles by task ID, not by comparing prompt wording: two differently worded requests can be the same work.

reason: Merge security and termination constraints of delegation because both must travel with the same child task.

title: Latency and the critical path
summary: A task's total time (its latency) is set by its **critical path**: the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another, including queueing, model and tool calls, retries, and checks. Steps running in parallel count only as long as the slowest one. To cut latency, first remove calls, then run independent steps in parallel, cache, stream the reply, and use smaller models where quality allows.

blocks.text:
`total = queue + sum(steps in sequence) + slowest(parallel steps) + coordination`

Below, the two reads don't depend on each other. Running them together saves 2 seconds (the shorter read), not 6, because the model step still waits for the slower read.

figure.title: One task, reads in sequence vs. in parallel
figure.caption: Example seconds. Parallel: 1 + max(2, 4) + 4 + 1 = 10 s, versus 12 s in sequence.

blocks.text:
To reduce latency, roughly in this order:

1. **Remove work:** drop unneeded model calls, merge small ones, stop resending repeated context.
2. **Run independent steps in parallel.**
3. **Cache** what is safe to reuse (see *Caching safely*).
4. **Use a smaller, faster model** where it meets the quality bar.
5. **Stream** the final reply, so the user sees it as it's written.

sections.title: Why many parallel branches hurt the slowest requests

blocks.text:
Averages hide the slow cases, so measure **percentiles**. **p95** is the time that 95% of requests finish within; the slowest few percent are the **tail latency**.

Parallel work finishes when its slowest branch does, and the more branches you start, the likelier one is slow. If each branch has a 1% chance of being slow, the chance that at least one of 10 is slow is 1 − 0.99^10 ≈ 9.6%.

figure.title: Combining results waits for the slowest branch
figure.caption: The average branch takes about 4.7 s, but combining can't start until 9 s.

blocks.text: To control the tail: cap the number of branches, give each a deadline, and return a clearly labeled partial result when the task allows it. For slow **reads** only, you can send a **hedged request**: a duplicate sent to another server, keeping whichever reply arrives first.

reason: Merge sequential latency, optimization advice, and parallel tail latency into one critical-path lesson.

title: Cost per task
summary: Add up everything a task costs (model tokens, tool and search calls, infrastructure, retries, and human review), then divide total spending by the number of verified successful outcomes. Human review and failed attempts often cost more than the tokens, so optimize the whole process, not the price of each call.

blocks.text: The prices below are made up; use your provider's current prices and your own measured usage.

per attempt:
  model:  6 calls, 18k input + 2.4k output tokens
          at $3 per million input, $15 per million output  = $0.054 + $0.036 = $0.090
  tools and search                                         = $0.010
  servers, storage, monitoring                             = $0.005
                                                           ≈ $0.105

per 100 attempts:
  attempts           100 × $0.105              = $10.50
  human review        10 escalations × $4.00    = $40.00
  verified outcomes  85 automatic + 10 reviewed = 95
  cost per outcome   $50.50 / 95                ≈ $0.53
code.caption: Human review is about 80% of the cost here: halving escalations saves more than halving the token bill.

blocks.text: After each change, confirm the verified success rate held. A smaller token bill isn't a saving if more results need fixing by hand.

title: Caching safely
summary: Many things can be cached: the fixed start of a prompt, document embeddings, stable tool results, and some search results. Whether a cached value is still valid depends on its sources, the user's permissions, and the prompt and model versions, so build these into the cache key and the rules for discarding entries. Never treat a cached confirmation as proof that a new action happened.

blocks.text: Each cache needs a key that captures what makes the value valid, and a rule for when to throw it away. A **TTL** (time to live) is how long an entry stays valid before it expires.

table.title: What can be cached
rows: Fixed prompt start (system prompt, tool list)
User's permissions, sources, prompt and model version
Never as proof of a new action

sections.title: A cache hit still needs a permission check

blocks.text: A cache keyed only by tenant and query will serve one user's answer to a colleague who isn't allowed to see its sources.

code.title: Permission-aware cache
code.text:
key   = (tenant, permissions_version, normalize(query),
         source_versions, prompt_version, model_version)
entry = cache.get(key)
if entry and not entry.expired and acl.can_read_all(user, entry.sources):
    return entry.value
value = compute_from_allowed_sources()
cache.put(key, value, ttl = freshness_limit)
code.caption: Discard entries when sources, permissions, or policies change. A TTL alone reacts too slowly to removed access.

reason: Retain caching as a correctness and access-control lesson, not only a performance recommendation.

title: Rate limits and fair scheduling
summary: Model providers impose **rate limits**: caps on requests and tokens per minute. Track every limit a call can hit, and reserve capacity before calling. Stop one tenant from starving the others with a queue per tenant, fair turn-taking, and capacity set aside for interactive users.

blocks.text: Staying under the request limit isn't enough, because a few very long prompts can use up the token limit. And with many workers, each sees the same "remaining capacity" and they all spend it at once, so reserve it atomically.

code.title: Reserving rate-limit capacity
code.text:
provider    = choose_allowed_provider(task)            # privacy and quality first
reservation = limiter.reserve(provider, tenant,
                              requests = 1, tokens = estimate_tokens(task))  # atomic
if not reservation: return queue_with_deadline(task)
result = provider.call(task, max_output_tokens = task.output_cap)
limiter.settle(reservation, actual = result.usage)     # correct the estimate
code.caption: Still obey the provider's “too many requests” (429) replies and the wait time they ask for; estimates drift from reality.

sections.title: One tenant must not take everything

blocks.text:
Tenant A submits 10,000 batch tasks. A moment later, tenant B sends one interactive request. With a single first-come, first-served queue, B waits behind all 10,000. Instead:

- **A queue per tenant,** served in fair turns.
- **Per-tenant caps** on parallel calls, tokens, and spending.
- **Capacity reserved for interactive work,** so batch jobs can't take all of it.
- **A clear overload rule:** reject, postpone, or queue with a deadline. Never wait forever.

Watch the **age** of the oldest queued task, not just the queue's length: 100 queued tasks are fine if the oldest is 2 seconds old.

reason: Merge provider rate limits and tenant fairness around a single admission-control boundary.

title: Scaling and capacity planning
summary: Scale by adding replaceable workers that take tasks from a durable queue, and add or remove workers based on queue age and backlog. Worker count is rarely the real bottleneck, though; model rate limits, other services, and the database usually are. Estimate the load with **Little's law**, then confirm with load tests.

blocks.text:
- Workers keep no state of their own (chapter 5), so you can add or remove them at any time.
- Keep cheap coordinating workers separate from expensive environments such as sandboxes or GPUs; they grow differently.
- Scale on **queue age** and backlog, not CPU use. An agent worker mostly waits on other services.
- A task waiting for approval or a slow tool should release its worker, not hold it.
- Adding workers without more capacity downstream just turns waiting into timeouts and retries.
Little's law: average number of tasks in the system = arrival rate × average time each task spends in it.

code.title: A first estimate
code.text:
arrival rate            = 2 tasks per second
average time in system  = 15 s
tasks in the system     = 2 × 15 = 30            # on average, under steady load

model calls per task    = 6, each about 1 s
model calls in progress ≈ 2 tasks/s × 6 calls × 1 s = 12 at a time, on average
code.caption: These are averages. Plan headroom for bursts and long tasks.

blocks.text: Averages don't tell you how many workers meet a p95 target. Load-test with realistic bursts, long tasks, large prompts, many tool calls, and failures. Then decide what happens when capacity runs out: turn work away, queue it with a deadline, or offer reduced service.

reason: Merge horizontal scaling and capacity planning; keep the distinction between average concurrency and required capacity.

title: Provider outages and graceful degradation
summary: When a model provider fails, notice quickly, save the task's progress, and switch only to a backup that meets the same privacy, location, and quality requirements. If none does, postpone the task. **Graceful degradation** means keeping the parts that still work running, and saying clearly what can't be done right now.

blocks.text: A **circuit breaker** stops calling a failing service for a while, instead of waiting on it again and again. A backup that is available but sends EU data outside the EU isn't a backup; it's an incident.

code.title: Fallback that keeps the rules
code.caption: If a timed-out call might have done something, reconcile it before starting replacement work.

blocks.text: Keep the parts whose services still work, and say plainly which parts don't.

table.title: What still works as services fail
rows: Compare options and book with approval
Compare options; save a proposed trip
Show order status from the orders system; queue the request
An answer from a model that isn't allowed

reason: Merge provider outages and graceful degradation, preserving privacy and honest outcome reporting through failure.

title: Multi-region failover
summary: When moving work to a backup region, move ownership as well as data. Before the backup resumes tasks, block the old region from writing, accept that the last few seconds of copied data may be missing, and reconcile actions that were in progress. Data-location rules apply to the backup region too.

blocks.text:
A broken network link doesn't stop the old region. It may still be running and writing, which is exactly how two regions end up issuing the same refund.

1. **Detect** that region A has failed or can't be reached.
2. **Block** region A: raise the ownership number so services reject A's writes (the fencing idea from *Stop stale workers with fencing tokens*).
3. **Load** the copied state in region B. Recent changes may be missing, up to your RPO (see below).
4. **Reconcile** in-progress actions by operation ID with each provider. Treat "unknown" as unknown.
5. **Resume** unfinished tasks. Pending approvals stay pending.

Set two targets. The **RPO** (recovery point objective) is how much recent data you can afford to lose, such as the last 5 seconds. The **RTO** (recovery time objective) is how long recovery may take. Then rehearse failover with pending approvals, payments in progress, copy delays, and a dependency that's down.

If ownership can't be established safely, pausing all writes is the right outcome. An uptime target never justifies paying twice, or processing data in a region where it isn't allowed.

reason: Retain regional recovery as a distinct application of ownership, replication, residency, and reconciliation.

title: Logs, metrics, and traces
summary: **Metrics** are counts and rates over time, showing how widespread a problem is. **Logs** record individual events. A **trace** follows one task across every model, policy, and tool call. Link all three with task and operation IDs, and record what the agent decided and did, not its internal reasoning.

blocks.text: Each answers a different question.

table.title: Metrics, logs, traces
rows: What happened in this one event?
Where did this task spend its time, and where did it fail?

blocks.text: A trace is made of **spans**: one timed entry per step, such as a model call, a policy check, or a tool call.

code.title: One task's trace
code.text:
task t-9  refund@14  refund-agent@31  model-x-2026-09          8.4 s
├─ model.decide        3.1k in / 120 out tokens                    1.2 s
├─ tool get_order(42)  op-5   OK                                   0.3 s
├─ model.decide        3.4k in / 90 out                            1.1 s
├─ policy.check        issue_refund $80 → NEEDS_APPROVAL           0.02 s
│   … waiting for approval (not counted as active time)
└─ tool issue_refund   op-42  TIMEOUT → lookup → OK, receipt R-981  5.6 s

blocks.text:
For each span, record the versions in use, token counts, duration, error codes, the decision, the proposed call, the policy result, and links to sources. Connect spans across agents with the parent task ID.

Prefer IDs and summaries over full prompts and documents (see *Audit trails without leaking data*). Monitor the decisions and actions you can observe; don't build monitoring that depends on reading a model's internal reasoning.

reason: Merge telemetry signals and tracing, with a concrete trace and the distinction between execution evidence and private model reasoning.

title: SLOs and what to do when they're missed
summary: An **SLO** (service-level objective) is a target for something you measure (speed, verified success, uptime, how quickly people pick up escalations) over a set group of requests and time window. Each missed target triggers an action decided in advance. Safety violations are not SLOs: their target is zero, and every single one is an incident.

blocks.text: Define exactly what counts: which tasks are included, what "success" means, how tasks waiting on users or approvals are handled, and over what period.

table.title: Example SLOs
rows: Escalations picked up by a person
Zero: each one is an incident
table.caption: Set targets from what the product needs and from what you measure today. Background jobs and interactive requests need different measures.

blocks.text:
A 99.9% uptime target allows 0.1% failure in its period; that allowance is the **error budget**. Using it up fast is a signal to act. Missing a target should trigger a decision made beforehand, not a debate:

- **Error budget burning fast:** alert the owner and pause any rollout in progress.
- **Success below target on one route:** switch that route back to the previous version or a backup.
- **Too slow because of load:** accept less batch work.
- **Any unauthorized action:** start incident response and use the kill switch for that action (see *Kill switches and incident response*).

Link every alert to example traces, so investigation starts from evidence.

reason: Keep operational SLO definitions distinct from the earlier business-outcome measures and release gates.

title: Quality drift and debugging regressions
summary: Quality can slowly change (drift) as models, prompts, tools, documents, and users change. Test continuously on two sets: a fixed set, which shows whether **your system** changed, and fresh samples of real traffic, which show whether **the work** changed. When success drops after a release, limit the damage first, then find what changed and reproduce the failure safely.

blocks.text:
Many things drift: the model (a provider update), prompts, tools, source documents, permissions, and what users ask for.

- Run the **fixed set** on a schedule to see whether your system changed on the same work.
- Score **sampled real tasks** with the same checks to see whether the work changed.

Break both down by task type and version, so you can see where a drop is.

sections.title: Example: success drops right after a release

blocks.text:
1. **Check it's real.** Is the sample big enough? Did the measurement itself change?
2. **Limit the damage.** If the impact is serious, roll back or send traffic to the previous version now, and investigate afterwards.
3. **Find what changed:** prompt, model, tools, policy, data, or the mix of requests. Break success down by version and task type.
4. **Compare traces.** Put failing and passing runs side by side, and find the first step where they differ.
5. **Reproduce** in a test environment using recorded tool results, so nothing real is changed.
6. **Fix and protect.** Add the failing cases to the golden set, then release again through the release checks.

sections.title: Debugging failures that come and go

blocks.text:
The same input can pass once and fail the next time, because model output varies.

- Record what's needed to re-run a task: inputs, versions, model outputs, and tool results.
- Re-run with the recorded tool results, so only the model varies.
- Run the failing case many times to measure **how often** it fails; one passing re-run proves nothing.
- If the model or outside data has changed since, exact reproduction may be impossible. Capture the failure pattern in a new test instead.

reason: Merge drift monitoring, nondeterministic debugging, and the deployment-regression scenario into one detection-to-repair workflow.

title: Kill switches and incident response
summary: A **kill switch** is a setting, outside the model, that immediately stops a capability or workflow from taking new actions. The scheduler checks it before starting work, and the tool gateway checks it before every action, so the model doesn't need to cooperate. Incident response then keeps the evidence, reconciles actions already in progress, fixes the cause, and restarts gradually.

blocks.text: Check it at two points: before work starts, and right before every action.

code.title: Kill-switch checks
code.text:
scheduler.before_start(task):
    require settings.enabled(task.workflow, task.tenant)

tool_gateway.before_action(call):
    require settings.enabled(call.capability)     # e.g. "issue_refund"
    require fence_is_current(call.task_id)
code.caption: If the settings service can't be reached, block actions (“fail closed”). A payment already accepted still needs reconciling.

blocks.text: Make switches fine-grained: one action (refunds), one workflow, one tenant, or everything. A switch that can only stop everything gets used too late, because flipping it costs too much.

1. **Find the scope:** which tasks, tenants, data, and actions are affected?
2. **Contain:** flip the right switch; stop accepting new work if needed.
3. **Keep evidence:** traces, audit records, versions.
4. **Reconcile** in-progress and uncertain actions by operation ID.
5. **Fix the cause** and add tests for it.
6. **Restart gradually,** with an owner and clear conditions, watching the rule that broke.

reason: Merge kill switches and incident response into a concrete containment-and-recovery sequence.

title: Audit trails without leaking data
summary: An **audit trail** is an append-only record of who asked for what, what was proposed, what the policy and approvers decided, and what actually happened, with versions and times. Keep it complete enough to reconstruct events but lean: by default record IDs and summaries rather than content, never keys or passwords, and send any sensitive content through a separate, restricted path that is deleted quickly.

blocks.text: Enough to answer "why did this money move?" months later.

code.title: An audit record
code.text:
audit.append({
    time, task_id, operation_id,
    actor: {user_id, agent_service}, tenant_id,
    versions: {workflow, prompt, model, policy},
    proposal_fingerprint, policy_decision, approval_id,
    observed_outcome               # e.g. receipt R-981, or "unknown, reconciling"
})
code.caption: Store it so entries can be added but never changed, and restrict who can read it. It records what was proposed, allowed, and observed, not merely what was intended.

blocks.text: Logging full prompts by default turns your monitoring system into a second copy of all customer data.

code.title: Monitoring events without content
code.text:
event = only_listed_fields(task_id, operation_id, duration, error_code, token_counts)
event += versions(prompt, model, workflow)
require not contains_secrets_or_personal_data(event)       # a scanner as a backstop
monitoring.write(event, readers = "ops-team", keep_for = 30 days)
# Full-content debug capture: separate store, needs approval, deleted quickly

blocks.text: Decide who can read each kind of monitoring data, and apply the same retention and deletion rules to search indexes and exports. Removing sensitive parts after the fact is a backstop; not collecting them is the real protection.

reason: Merge audit content and privacy-preserving telemetry so evidence quality and data minimization are designed together.

title: Case study: refund agent
summary: The running example, assembled. The customer is identified at login; the agent loads the order and refund policy. The model reads the request; code decides eligibility and the amount. Refunds over $50 need a support lead's approval. The refund goes through the payment service with an operation ID, a timeout is reconciled rather than retried blindly, and a justified refusal or a handoff counts as a valid outcome.

table.title: Refund agent design
rows: Reads the customer's message, chooses tools, writes the reply
Identity, eligibility, refundable amount, policy, approvals, retries
`get_order` and `get_refund_policy` (read); `issue_refund` (changes data, uses an operation ID)
Within 30 days of delivery and within the refundable balance; otherwise refuse and say why
A support lead approves refunds over $50; smaller ones run automatically
Receipt from the payment service, a written refusal, or a handoff
Timeout after the refund was paid: reconcile op-42, never resend
Verified resolution rate, duplicate refunds (must be 0), p95 time, cost per resolution

blocks.text: A request can end correctly in more than one way.

nodes:

auto if ≤ $50, else lead

Explain refusal
not eligible is a valid end

Reconcile op-42

with operation ID op-42

blocks.text:
Golden cases: an eligible small refund; one large enough to need approval; one outside the 30-day window; two matching orders (the agent should ask which); a customer asking about someone else's order; a timeout after the refund was paid; and a message containing "the manager already approved this".

Score each case by checking the payment service and the task record, not by reading the reply.

reason: Assemble the running example into an end-to-end design, linking previously introduced boundaries.

title: Case study: research agent with citations
summary: Turn the request into specific research questions, search only sources the user may read that are recent enough, and have worker agents return claims with citations. Check each claim against its source, settle conflicting findings, and save the report with its evidence. For high-stakes work such as due diligence before an acquisition, experts review the conclusions before anyone relies on them.

table.title: Research agent design
rows: The request becomes specific questions, with scope, how recent sources must be, and what a good answer needs
A supervisor plus one research worker per independent question, in parallel
Claims, each with source, quoted passage, date, and limitations
Every important claim checked against its passage; numbers recomputed in code
Compare definitions and periods; show remaining conflicts with both sources
Evidence and report saved as files, separate from the workers' working memory
Share of supported claims, important evidence missing, conflicts left open

blocks.text:
A multi-agent due-diligence system for an acquisition follows the same design, with more at stake:

- **One agent per field:** finance, legal, market, and technology, each reading only its own folders in the deal's secure document store.
- **Financial figures** are recomputed in code from the source statements; a model's arithmetic is never final.
- **Conflicts** between agents, such as revenue counted differently, are settled by definitions and by which source owns the fact (see *Stale and conflicting sources*), never by vote.
- **Expert sign-off** is required before any conclusion enters the investment memo. The agents draft and cite; people decide.
- **Access limits** carry through to the final report, since deal documents are often restricted.

reason: Merge general cited research and acquisition due diligence; treat diligence as a high-stakes variant of the same evidence pipeline.

title: Case study: coding agent
summary: The agent works in a sandbox on its own code branch and can change only that branch. It reads the project's instructions and code, makes the change, runs the project's checks, and opens a pull request with the changes, the reasoning, and honest test results. Merging and releasing stay with people.

table.title: Coding agent design
rows: A fresh sandbox with the repository on a new branch; network limited to approved sites
Push to its own branch; open pull requests. No merging, no releasing, no production keys.
Read instructions and code → plan → edit → build and test → fix → repeat, within limits
Issue text, code comments, test output, third-party code: data, not instructions
A pull request with the changes, why they were made, which checks ran and their results, and known limits
Pull requests merged without major rework; check pass rate; review time; changes later reverted

blocks.text:
- **Report checks honestly.** "Tests pass" must mean the agent ran them and they passed. If it couldn't run them, the pull request says so.
- **Keep actions separate:** pushing a branch, opening a pull request, merging, and releasing are four actions with four permission levels. Branch access implies none of the others.
- **Recover from facts:** after a crash, look at what actually exists (the branch, the pull request number), not at the agent's last message.
- **One owner per file** when several agents work on one change, or they overwrite each other's edits.

reason: Present the coding agent as an artifact-oriented design with a clear publication boundary.

title: Case study: answering questions from a database
summary: Settle what the question means (which revenue definition, which period, which currency) before writing SQL. Show the model only the tables the user may query, check the generated query's structure against rules, run it with a read-only account under limits on rows, time, and cost, and explain the result together with the query that produced it.

blocks.text: "Show revenue by region" is ambiguous: orders booked or revenue earned? Which quarter? Which currency? Ask, or use a documented default and say so in the answer. A **semantic layer**, a shared set of documented metric definitions the agent can look up, removes most of this ambiguity.

sections.title: Check the query, not the text

blocks.text: A query that starts with `SELECT` can still read a restricted table or scan a billion rows. Parse it into its structure and check that instead.

code.title: A limited query path
code.text:
tables = catalog.visible_to(user)                      # only allowed tables and columns
sql    = model.write_query(question, tables, metric_definitions)
parsed = sql_parser.parse(sql)                         # reject anything that doesn't parse
require query_rules.allow(parsed, user)                # tables, columns, no changes, row filters
result = readonly_db.run(parsed, as_user = user,       # database permissions as a backstop
                         max_rows = 10_000, timeout = 20 s, max_cost = budget)
return explain(result, query = sql, definitions_used, as_of = result.time)
code.caption: Read-only doesn't mean harmless: a query can expose restricted rows or overload the database.

blocks.text: Check that the result makes sense (units, row counts, missing values) before explaining it. If two definitions give different totals, show both instead of inventing one combined number.

reason: Organize the database case around ambiguity, query validation, bounded execution, and interpretable results.

title: Case study: incident-response assistant
summary: Start read-only: gather metrics, logs, traces, recent releases, and how services depend on each other; run known checks; and test each suspected cause against the evidence. Fixing, such as restarting or rolling back, is a separate step, limited to approved procedures (runbooks) and authorized by a person or an explicit rule, and followed by confirmation that the system actually recovered.

table.title: Incident assistant design
rows: An alert, such as checkout p95 latency above its SLO
Metrics, logs, traces, release history, service dependency map, runbooks (documented, pre-approved procedures)
Code checks for known problems first, then model-suggested causes, each tested
Plan, then replan as evidence arrives (chapter 4)
Approved runbook steps only (restart, roll back, add capacity), each authorized by a person or a rule
Confirm recovery with the same metrics; reconcile any action with an unknown result
Time to diagnosis, correct-cause rate, harmful-action rate (target 0), confirmed recoveries

blocks.text:
1. Collect evidence for the affected services and time window.
2. State a suspected cause, such as "release 4812 doubled database calls per request", and the check that would confirm or rule it out.
3. Run the check. A release that coincides with the problem is a lead, not proof.
4. Propose a fix with the services affected, the exact runbook command, the expected effect, and how success will be measured.
5. Once approved, run it, then confirm recovery from the metrics, not from the command's exit status.

If a restart's result is unclear, check the service before restarting again. Repeated automatic restarts can turn a partial outage into a full one.

reason: Present incident response as a diagnosis-to-fix sequence rather than another generic architecture list.

title: Case study: travel booking
summary: Search and compare offers, then present one concrete trip with prices and cancellation terms. Re-check price and availability just before booking, and ask for approval again if anything important changed. Book each part as a saga step with its own operation ID, reconcile uncertain bookings before cancelling anything, and always show the traveler exactly what is and isn't booked.

table.title: Travel agent design
rows: Flights and hotels within the traveler's preferences and budget, compared in one format
An exact trip: prices, fare rules, cancellation terms, total
Tied to the offer's fingerprint; a change in price or terms needs approval again
A saga: hotel → flight → payment, each with an operation ID and an undo action
Unknown result → reconcile first; confirmed failure → undo finished steps in reverse order
Booking service down → save the proposal and say clearly that nothing is booked

blocks.text:
Prices change between search and purchase. If the flight went from $420 to $480, the old approval doesn't cover it; ask again and show both prices.

If the hotel is booked and the flight call times out, don't cancel the hotel yet; look up the flight booking first. If the flight definitely failed, cancel the hotel under its rules, including any fee, and if that cancellation fails, hand the case to a person. Always show the traveler the full known state: "Hotel booked (confirmation H-77). Flight not booked. Hotel cancellation requested."

reason: Keep travel as the concrete distributed-saga walkthrough, emphasizing changed offers and uncertain partial success.

title: Case study: invoice processing
summary: Treat the fields the model extracts as suggestions. Check totals, supplier identity, duplicates, and the match with the purchase order in code against trusted systems. Send anything suspicious to a person along with the original document, and record the invoice in the accounting system with a fixed posting ID. Bank details found in a document never update a supplier's record directly.

table.title: Invoice agent design
rows: The model extracts supplier, invoice number, line items, totals, currency, and purchase-order number, with page locations
Lines add up to the total; supplier exists; invoice not already recorded; matches the purchase order within tolerance
Mismatches, new or changed bank details, unusual amounts: shown to a person next to the document
The accounting system, using posting ID `supplier:invoice_number`; it blocks duplicates and checks permissions
Document, accepted fields, check results, approvals, and accounting entry, linked together
Share handled with no human touch, recording errors, duplicates (must be 0), review time

blocks.text:
- **Changed bank details** on an invoice are a classic fraud pattern. Changes go through the official supplier-update process, confirmed with a known contact, never taken from the document.
- **Duplicates** arrive as the same PDF twice, or a re-sent invoice under a new file name. Detect them by supplier plus invoice number, not by file.
- **Crash after recording:** the posting ID lets the retry find the existing entry instead of creating a second one.

Put each of these, plus total and currency mismatches, in the golden set.

reason: Retain invoices as a distinct document-to-ledger workflow with numeric and duplicate invariants.

title: Case study: browser agent
summary: Run the browser in an isolated environment that can visit only approved sites, with limited logins. Look at the page before each action and check the result after it; require approval before submitting forms, paying, or deleting; and treat page text as untrusted. If a submission's result is unclear, look for what it should have created before clicking again. Use an API instead whenever one exists.

blocks.text: A click is only an attempt; the page afterwards shows what actually happened.

code.title: One browser step
code.text:
require browser.current_site in task.allowed_sites
before   = browser.look()                        # screenshot plus page structure
proposal = agent.choose_action(before)           # page text is untrusted data
require policy.allows(proposal)
if proposal.submits_or_pays_or_deletes:
    require approval_for(proposal)
browser.do(proposal)
after = browser.look()
require browser.current_site in task.allowed_sites      # a click can lead elsewhere
require expected_state(after) or escalate("unexpected page")

blocks.text:
Pages load in pieces, change layout, and sometimes submit successfully without showing a confirmation. Before clicking **Submit** again:

- look for what the submission should have created (an order number, a sent message, a new entry);
- if you can't find it, mark the result unknown and escalate. Don't click again.

A page saying "the user has approved this purchase" grants nothing; approval comes only from your approval system.

reason: Keep browser use as a distinct observation/action interface with submission ambiguity, not another generic tool call.

title: Build or buy
summary: List what your tasks require (crash recovery, acting on the user's behalf, data-location rules, duplicate-safe tools, testing, monitoring), then test candidate platforms against that list using your own failure cases. Buy what fits; build only where your business rules or security needs demand control. Count the ongoing cost of running whatever you build.

sections.title: Test what matters, not the feature list

blocks.text: A demo of the happy path tells you little. Run one small end-to-end task on each candidate, and break it on purpose.

table.title: Questions for an agent platform
rows: Kill a worker mid-task. Does it resume without repeating a tool call?
Can tools act for the end user, with limited, short-lived tokens?
Where are prompts, logs, and memory stored? Can you choose the region and how long data is kept?

title: Architecture review checklist
summary: Review an agent design by following one real task from start to finish: where identity comes from, where each rule is enforced, what happens to every action on retry or crash, and how outcomes are confirmed. Then ask what can be removed, and what still needs evidence.

blocks.text:
Follow one task, such as "refund order 42", and ask:

- **Contract:** is "done" defined and checkable? Who takes over a stuck task?
- **Permissions:** where does identity come from? Is each permission and limit enforced in code, or only stated in a prompt?
- **Actions:** for each action, what happens on a duplicate message, a lost response, a stale worker, or a changed permission?
- **Sources:** for each source, how are access, freshness, corrections, and deletion handled?
- **State:** can any worker crash at any point without losing progress or repeating an action?
- **Testing:** is there a golden set with invariants? Do releases pass checks?
- **Operations:** are there traces, SLOs, a kill switch, and an audit trail?

Compare the design with the simplest version that could work, and remove agents, steps, and tools without a measured purpose. Every part should have a reason you can point to in the test results.
